I Finally Bought a McLaren F1 in Gran Turismo 7 and Here's What I Did Next
25 photos
Photo: autoevolution
I just looked at my GT7 dashboard and realized I’ve spent nearly 700 hours in the game since I first got my hands on it a few years ago. It’s no longer as exciting to me as the two new Assetto Corsa titles (EVO and Rally) have more to offer from a driving perspective.
But Gran Turismo 7 still has plenty of advantages, including how easy it is for me to just use the controlled pad instead of installing and removing the Logitech RS50 system every single time.
That won’t be a problem once I’ll have my own room and sim rig, which won’t happen for at least a few months. However, I will likely keep playing GT7 at least until Polyphony Digital makes the switch to GT8.
I still have some unfinished business in here, which includes buying and driving every vehicle available. After today, I’m one step closer to that objective.
That’s because I could finally raise 20 million credits, which is what you’ll need to pay for the McLaren F1 GTR. Before I show you what its first mission was, let me tell you a few things about the latest Weekly Challenges.
Jimny Cup Photo: autoevolution It wasn’t that long ago that we had another event in the Jimny Cup. I had a bad time driving my highly-tuned model with just under 300 hp on tap. I noticed a few other players reported a similar experience, and it might all be a result of all the physics tweaks Polyphony has done recently.
I promised myself I wouldn’t use that setup ever again, which is why I bought a brand-new Jimny for today’s three-lap race in Canada.
I figured 112 bhp would be enough, considering I also bought a weight-reduction package. The Castrol livery felt like a good match for the off-road adventure. Even though I almost fell asleep during the race because of how slow this car is, it was still a better experience compared to last time’s outing.
Scoring 52,500 credits after four minutes and 20 seconds, there was only one question on my mind: will we ever get another snow-covered track in GT7 before support for the game stops? At least I know a surprise like that is coming to Assetto Corsa Rally soon.
Special Event Photo: autoevolution I had just recently V12-swapped my Honda Step WGN for a few laps around Barcelona-Catalunya ahead of the latest Time Trial . With all the chassis upgrades and RS tires on, it was pretty good for its size.
I realized using the same setup for this Special Event might be too much, but I also didn’t want to buy another car and start from scratch. Plus, I curious to see how fast I could go through Suzuka’s iconic 130R corner.
What I failed to realize was that this four-lap battle was about to occur around the East Course layout which is much shorter than the full course. I was in the lead just 45 seconds after the start, and found myself lapping everyone at the beginning of Lap 4.
I’d say this car feels a bit wobbly with all that power (and brakes), but I’d still an engine swap I’d recommend to a friend. You’re looking at a 45,000-credits payout after three and a half minutes of racing, by the way.
European Clubman Cup 600 Photo: autoevolution The European Clubman Cup 600 isn’t just about cars built in Europe: it also takes us over to the fictional Dragon Trail-Seaside Reverse track for four laps. I thought about using my tuned Ferrari F355 for the job, but it was way over the suggested 600 PP limit.
I was keen to get back into a Porsche , and my stock 997 GT3 was just waiting for it to happen. Well, I increased the horsepower output and reduced the overall weight before the race, and then found a stunning recreation of what might be the only 997 GT3 RS 4.0 finished in Aston Martin specific color.
Thank God window shopping doesn’t cost a cent. I needed almost three minutes to take the lead, and finished the race four and a half minutes later.
After scoring 75,000 credits for the deed, I noticed my fastest lap in this car was almost half a second quicker than the world record for the recent Lexus RC F Time Trial at the same track.
Evolution Meeting Photo: autoevolution Ever since living with RWD cars, I’ve began losing interest in Mitsubishi Lancer EVOs and Subaru Impreza WRX STIs. I’d still want one for some snow fun, but I would much rather drive an FR platform anywhere else.
This Evolution Meeting event is scheduled for Monza, where you’ll fight 11 other opponents for a total of four laps. I had an Evo IX for the job, complete with 511 bhp on tap and weighing a mere 2,440 lbs/1,107 kg.
There are two pages of time attack themed liveries to choose from, and I didn’t want to keep using my old Cyber EVO one. Hitting 180 mph/290 kph before Turn 1 was great, having to back off the throttle in the first right-hand corner after the chicane due to severe understeer was not.
Am I the only one who thinks Sugo should have been on the menu this week, too? Anyway, I only needed just under eight minutes for the whole event, and was happy to walk away with 105,000 credits thanks to the Clean Race Bonus.
World Touring Car 900 Photo: autoevolution Interlagos is longer than Sugo, yes, but I still support the idea the latest track in the game could have been the right spot for this World Touring Car 900 event. Imagine running there for 15 or 16 laps total! Since I recently unlocked a 2008 Honda NSX GT500, I wanted to use it for this last race of the Weekly Challenges.
At 796 PP, it’s certainly not the fastest Group 2 car in the game. And it looks simply stunning with the Spoon livery, doesn’t it? I found myself in a strange situation two or three laps into the whole thing: some driver hit the wall right in front of me, we got a yellow flag, and I couldn’t slow my car down in time to avoid a three-second penalty.
I stopped for gas and new tires after eight laps, only to discover I had forgotten to buy the grippiest compound available. Regardless of how hard I tried, I couldn’t close the gap to the leader and ultimately finished 20 seconds after he did.
You will still score 102,000 credits for that kind of result, plus the 500K bonus that comes with getting a podium in all five events. But it’s now bugging me so badly that I just need to go at it again.
McLaren F1 Race Car & Nurburgring Nordschleife Photo: autoevolution I had to sell four of my top-tier cars to afford buying the McLaren F1 GTR. I didn’t care about the Ford Mark IV Race Car or the Corvette Racer Concept, but letting go of the Jaguar XJ13 wasn’t easy. Also, I can always get another Ferrari 499P relatively easy, so that’s not that big of a problem either.
I refrained from selling the Ferrari F40 and the Mercedes CLK-LM, though! I can’t believe it took me so long to buy my first 20 million credits car in GT7. I’m almost certain it used to cost half as much a few years ago, but I’ll have to dig through the archives to get a clear answer.
With 600 bhp on tap and weighing just 2,315 lbs (1,050 kg), this is technically a Group 3 race car. The Harrods livery is still my go-to option for it, and it kind of fits the Green Hell if you think about it. It’s quite a beast out there, although it could benefit from more aero. I couldn’t go flat out through Flugpatz and even crashed while trying to do so.
I only needed four minutes to reach the Karoussel, and 6:44 for the complete lap. That’s eight seconds slower than what I achieved in my tuned 911 GT1. I’m sure switching to a turbocharged setup is an easy fix for that.
